docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
A simulation produces a lot of numbers: loop positions, epigenetic states, energies, and thousands of 3D structures. A metric is a single number (or one number per sample) that summarises one aspect of them, so that runs, phases and parameter values can be compared. This page defines every metric RepliSage computes, in the notation of the paper, and says whether it is inferred from the Monte Carlo (the graph: loops and epigenetic states) or from the molecular dynamics (the 3D coordinates). The results are in the report and in metadata/; see Analysis for how to read a run.

Two sources of metrics

Monte Carlo (MC) metrics are computed from the sampled graph: where the LEF legs are, which state each bead has, the energies and the replication fork positions. They are cheap and exist for every sample.

Molecular dynamics (MD) metrics are computed from the 3D bead coordinates of each structure, which exist only when the 3D part ran. They describe size, shape and contacts, and are the ones you can compare with microscopy and Hi-C.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(N\) number of beads (one bead = a genomic segment, see bead_kb in the report) \(T\) number of recorded samples (one every MC_STEP Monte Carlo steps) \((m_k, n_k)\) the two legs of LEF \(k\); \(m_k < n_k\) when bound, \(m_k = n_k = -1\) when unbound \(\ell_k = n_k - m_k\) length of the loop of LEF \(k\), in beads (\(0\) if unbound) \(s_i \in \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\) epigenetic state of bead \(i\) (positive = A-like, negative = B-like) \(r_i\) 3D position of bead \(i\) in one structure (a vector with three coordinates) \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) average (over beads, samples or structures, stated in each case) \(\#\{\cdot\}\) number of items that satisfy the condition inside

All MC quantities are computed per recorded sample \(t\), so each metric is a time series. Phase values (G1, S, G2/M) are means of that series over the samples of the phase, and the report also gives the standard deviation. Because consecutive samples are correlated, this standard deviation describes fluctuations and is not an uncertainty.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
Loop length. For one sample, the mean loop length is the average of \(n_k - m_k\) over all LEFs, so an unbound LEF counts as length 0 (this is the definition used in the paper). The bound loop length averages only over the bound LEFs. Multiply by the bead size to get kilobases. The report also gives the median and the 95th percentile of the bound loop lengths.

Fraction of bound LEFs. A LEF is bound when \(m_k \ge 0\) and \(n_k > m_k\), so

\[f_{\text{bound}} = \frac{\#\{\text{bound LEFs}\}}{N_{\text{lef}}}\]

Legs on CTCF sites. The fraction of bound LEFs whose left leg sits on a CTCF site that attracts left legs, \(f_L\), and whose right leg sits on a site that attracts right legs, \(f_R\) (the orientation of the sites is explained in the biology page). They tell how strongly the loops are anchored.

Coverage. The number of loops that span bead \(i\), that is the number of bound LEFs with \(m_k \le i < n_k\). The report gives the fraction of beads covered by at least one loop and the mean coverage (loops per bead). A very high mean coverage with short loops is the signature of stacking, many loops piled on the same place, which is what happens when \(T_{\text{mc}}\) is too low (see the critical region).

docs.title: Energies
docs.text:
The Monte Carlo energy is split into its terms, each recorded per sample (the terms are defined in the Monte Carlo model):

Metric Meaning Total energy \(\mathcal{H}\) sum of all terms Folding energy loop-size term (favours long loops) Binding energy CTCF term (favours legs on CTCF sites) Epigenetic energy state-field, neighbour and loop-anchor terms (only with replication data)

After burn-in the energy should fluctuate around a flat line. The acceptance rate (the fraction of accepted proposals) is reported too; the report warns when it is below 10 % or above 60 %.

docs.title: Replication and loops
docs.text:
Loops are not allowed to straddle a replication fork. Let \(f_i(t) = 1\) if bead \(i\) is replicated at time \(t\) and \(0\) if not. A loop \((m, n)\) is a violation if its two legs are in different replication states (\(f_m \ne f_n\)), or if both legs are replicated but some bead between them is not. The number of violations is counted in S phase, and each violating loop has a strength

\[\sigma = \min(r,\ \ell - r) + 1\]

where \(\ell = n - m\) is the loop length and \(r\) the number of replicated beads inside it. The reported strength is the sum of \(\sigma\) over the violating loops divided by (their number + 1). A good S phase has violations near zero.

docs.title: Epigenetic states and compartments
docs.text:
Average epigenetic state. The mean state over all beads, \(\langle s \rangle\). It is close to 0 when A-like and B-like beads balance, and its change in S phase shows a global shift.

State fractions. \(p_k\) is the fraction of beads in state \(k\), for \(k = -2, \dots, 2\).

Compartment of a bead. In a window of samples (the first and the last 10 % of S phase), take the mean state \(\bar{s}_i\) of each bead and classify it:

Window-mean state Compartment \(\bar{s}_i > 0.25\) A (active) \(\bar{s}_i < -0.25\) B (inactive) in between N (neutral)

Compartment switching. Comparing the two windows gives a \(3 \times 3\) table of how many beads go from B, N or A to B, N or A. The report lists the number of beads that switched B to A and A to B, the net flux (B to A minus A to B), the fraction of unchanged beads and the A and B fractions before and after. For the time series, the switching rate at lag \(\tau\) is the fraction of beads that have a negative state at sample \(t\) and a positive state at sample \(t + \tau\) (B to A), and the reverse for A to B.

docs.title: Order parameters of the epigenetic states
docs.text:
These describe how ordered the states are at each sample (only with replication data). With \(q = 5\) states, \(p_k\) the fraction of beads in state \(k\) and \(p_{\max}\) the largest of them:

Metric Definition Meaning Magnetisation \(M = \dfrac{q\,p_{\max} - 1}{q - 1}\) 0 if the states are evenly mixed, 1 if all beads share one state Cluster order \(C = p_{\max}\) the fraction of beads in the most common state (state counts, not neighbours along the chain) Binder-type cumulant \(U = 1 - \dfrac{\sum_k p_k^4}{3\,(\sum_k p_k^2)^2}\) a measure of the shape of the state distribution (built from its second and fourth moments) Entropy \(H = -\sum_k p_k \ln p_k\) 0 if all beads share a state, \(\ln q\) if the states are evenly mixed Synchronisation \(\dfrac{\text{fraction of edges whose two beads have the same state}}{q - 1}\) agreement of the states of beads joined by an edge of the graph

For the synchronisation, the graph has one edge between every pair of consecutive beads and one edge for every bound loop, so it measures how well neighbouring beads and the two anchors of a loop agree, which is what produces compartments. The fraction is divided by \(q - 1\), so with \(q = 5\) the value stays between 0 and 0.25. Use it for comparisons between phases and runs, not as an absolute fraction.

docs.title: Replication simulation
docs.text:
These come from the replication simulation (Replikator), not from the loops. With \(f_i(t)\) as above (1 = replicated):

Metric Definition Replicated fraction \(F(t)\) = fraction of beads with \(f_i(t) = 1\) Replication time of bead \(i\) \(t_i\) = first time with \(f_i = 1\), divided by the S-phase length (0 to 1) \(T_{10}\), \(T_{50}\), \(T_{90}\) the times at which \(F\) first reaches 10 %, 50 % and 90 % S-phase span \(T_{90} - T_{10}\), how spread out the replication is Inferred origins local minima of the profile \(t_i\) Median origin spacing median distance between neighbouring origins, in kb Agreement with the input Spearman correlation \(\rho\) between \(t_i\) and the input timing (early beads should replicate early)

docs.title: Convergence diagnostics
docs.text:
These tell whether the Monte Carlo has run long enough, and are applied to the series above (energies, loop lengths, bound fraction, average state): autocorrelation \(\rho(\tau)\), integrated autocorrelation time \(T_\rho\), effective sample size \(n_{\text{eff}} = n / T_\rho\), standard error \(\mathrm{MCSE} = s / \sqrt{n_{\text{eff}}}\), the Geweke \(z\) score and the split \(\hat{R}\). They are defined in Analysis and explained in Monte Carlo, MCMC and Metropolis.

Effect size between phases. To say how much an observable changes from G1 to S, the report gives Cohen's \(d\),

\[d = \frac{\mu_{\text{S}} - \mu_{\text{G1}}}{\sigma_{\text{pooled}}}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{pooled}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\text{G1}}^2 + \sigma_{\text{S}}^2}{2}}\]

where \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are the mean and standard deviation of the observable in each phase. As a rule of thumb, \(d\) below 0.2 (in absolute value) is small and above 0.8 is large.

docs.title: Metrics from the 3D structures
docs.text: For every structure the coordinates form a matrix \(V\) of \(N\) rows (beads) and three columns. With replication there are two chains (the two sister chromatids). The shape and size metrics below are computed on the first sister, and a few extra ones use both. Coordinates are in Å in the structure files, and the figures convert lengths to nm and volumes to nm\(^3\).

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
Let \(c\) be the centre of mass (the mean of all \(r_i\)), \(D_i\) the distance of bead \(i\) from it, and \(d_{ij}\) the distance between beads \(i\) and \(j\).

Metric Definition Meaning Radius of gyration \(R_g = \sqrt{\langle D_i^2 \rangle}\) root-mean-square distance from the centre: the overall size Mean distance to the centre \(\langle D_i \rangle\) radial spread Maximum distance to the centre \(\max_i D_i\) the farthest bead Mean pairwise distance \(\langle d_{ij} \rangle\) over all pairs compactness Standard deviation of pairwise distances spread of \(d_{ij}\) over all pairs how heterogeneous the structure is Maximum pairwise distance \(\max d_{ij}\) the diameter End-to-end distance \(d_{1N}\) distance between the two chain ends

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
The gyration tensor \(G\) describes how the beads are spread in each direction. It is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix whose entry \(G_{ab}\) is the average over beads of (offset from the centre along axis \(a\)) times (offset along axis \(b\)). Its eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3 \ge 0\) are the squared extents along the three principal axes, and they add up to \(R_g^2\). A sphere has three equal eigenvalues, a rod has one large, and a flat disc has one small.

Metric Definition Meaning Asphericity \(\dfrac{\lambda_1 - \lambda_3}{R_g^2}\) 0 for a sphere, towards 1 for an elongated shape (the definition used in RepliSage, which differs from the usual \(\lambda_1 - \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_2 + \lambda_3)\) form) Planarity \(\dfrac{\lambda_3}{R_g^2}\) small for a flat shape, up to \(1/3\) for a sphere Ellipsoid ratio \(\sqrt{\lambda_1 / \lambda_3}\) longest over shortest principal extent Ellipsoid volume \(\frac{4}{3}\pi \sqrt{\lambda_1 \lambda_2 \lambda_3}\) volume of the ellipsoid whose semi-axes are the principal extents

docs.title: Volume and contacts
docs.text: Metric Definition Meaning Convex hull volume volume of the smallest convex shape that contains all beads the space the structure occupies; falls when the structure compacts Bounding box volume width \(\times\) height \(\times\) depth volume of the axis-aligned box around the beads Contact number \(\langle \#\{j \ne i : d_{ij} < d_c\} \rangle_i\) mean number of beads closer than the cutoff \(d_c\) (default \(d_c = 1\) in coordinate units)

docs.title: Two chains: sisters
docs.text:
With replication, the whole system of both sisters has its own size and volume, and the two chromatids are compared:

Metric Definition Meaning Total radius of gyration, total convex hull volume \(R_g\) and hull volume computed on all \(2N\) beads size and volume of the replicated system Sister distance distance between the centroids of the two chains 0 when the sisters overlap, growing as they separate

docs.title: Contact maps
docs.text:
For a set of structures (all of one phase), the contact map is the average of an inverse distance,

\[C_{ij} = \left\langle \frac{1}{d_{ij} + 1} \right\rangle\]

where \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) averages over the structures and \(d_{ij}\) is the distance between beads \(i\) and \(j\) in one structure (high value = close). It is the 3D counterpart of a Hi-C map and is computed separately for G1, S and G2/M. Averaging the maps is preferred to taking the map of the average structure, because a mean structure is blurred and its distances are not those of any single cell.

docs.title: Available but not computed by default
docs.text: The code also contains the box-counting (fractal) dimension, the global distance fluctuation and a PCA-based structural anisotropy. They are slow on large structures and are off in the standard pipeline; you can call them from src/analysis/structure_metrics.py.

docs.title: Reading the metrics
docs.text:
• Loops getting shorter in S phase is expected, because forks act as barriers that loops may not cross; check that the violations stay near zero.
  • Compartment switching (a net flux from B to A) is expected when forks act as epigenetic organisers (REP_FORK_EPIGENETIC_ORGANIZER).
  • \(R_g\) and the convex hull volume should rise in S (replicated chromatin unfolds and the sisters form) and fall in G2/M (condensation). The sister distance rises when the sisters separate.
  • Order parameters help to spot when the system is too frozen or too noisy; they are one of the ways to choose \(T_{\text{mc}}\) in the critical region.
  • Trust trends and ratios between phases more than absolute values, because the model has arbitrary length and energy units, and in S phase the system is out of equilibrium (see the Hamiltonian idea).

docs.title: Microstates, macrostates and ensembles
docs.text: Statistical physics separates the detailed description of a system from the averaged description that we actually compare with experiments. This page explains the vocabulary and how it maps onto RepliSage.

docs.title: Microstate
docs.text:
A microstate is a complete specification of the system at one instant. In RepliSage, a microstate is the configuration

\[\mathcal{S} = \left(\{(m_i, n_i)\}_{i=1}^{N_{\text{lef}}},\ \{s_k\}_{k=1}^{N_{\text{beads}}}\right)\]

together with the state of replication \(f_{\text{rep}}(x,t)\) at that time: where every LEF leg sits, which state each bead has, and where every fork is. In the 3D part, the exact coordinates of the beads belong here too. There are astronomically many microstates, and each single one is of little use on its own, since a real cell population is a mixture of them.

docs.title: Macrostate
docs.text:
A macrostate is a description by a few averaged quantities that many microstates share. The paper uses exactly this language: compartmentalisation is a macrostate that emerges from the microstates (the individual epigenetic labels). Typical macrostates in RepliSage are:

  • an order parameter, such as the mean state \(\langle s \rangle\), the fraction of links that join beads of the same sign, or the mean loop length \(\langle \ell \rangle\);
  • the average contact heatmap, obtained by averaging over the ensemble;
  • the A/B compartment profile, from the mean epigenetic state of each bead;
  • structural summaries such as the radius of gyration \(R_g\).

Many different microstates give the same macrostate. For example, two different arrangements of LEFs can have the same mean loop length.

Beads are coloured by their state \(s_k\) (red for \(s_k>0\), blue for \(s_k<0\)), arcs are LEFs \((m_i, n_i)\) and the green ring marks the bead where a replication fork sits.

docs.title: Ensembles
docs.text:
An ensemble is the collection of microstates we sample, here the MCMC samples from all replicas. A macrostate is an average over the ensemble, \(\langle O \rangle\), as in Monte Carlo, MCMC and Metropolis. This is why RepliSage produces many structures per phase rather than one: the experiment (for example Hi-C) is itself an average over many cells.

Concept In RepliSage Example Microstate One sampled configuration positions of LEFs, epigenetic states, forks, bead coordinates Observable \(O(\mathcal{S})\) A function of a microstate loop length of this configuration Ensemble All samples from all replicas thousands of structures Macrostate Average of observables \(\langle \ell\rangle\), \(\langle s\rangle\), the average heatmap

docs.title: Equilibrium and S phase
docs.text:
In G1 and G2/M the rules do not change, so the ensemble is stationary and macrostates settle to constant values. In S phase the forks keep changing the rules, so the macrostates move with time: the mean loop length drops, and the average epigenetic state shifts as forks pass. The relevant averaging is over replicas at each time, not over time.

This is the main reason why RepliSage reports phase-wise means and uses several replicas (--n-replicas): see Analysis for how the report computes them, and Known limitations for what this does not capture.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
RepliSage is a chain of small stages. Each stage reads what the previous one produced, and the inputs you give decide which stages run. Every stage can also be run on its own from a script (see the bottom of each file in src/pipeline/).

Grey boxes always run; pink boxes run only when their inputs are present; blue boxes are inputs; yellow diamonds are decisions; the strong pink box is the final report.

docs.title: Time in a replicating run
docs.text:
For what each phase means biologically, see Scope and goals.

A cell cycle is laid out along the Monte Carlo steps. The first steps are burn-in, during which the system relaxes. G1 follows, then S phase from REP_START_TIME for REP_TIME_DURATION steps, then G2/M.

During S the replicated-DNA matrix tells the Monte Carlo which beads are already copied. The 3D model then has two chains (the sister chromatids) that are tied together where DNA is replicated and pulled apart after S.

docs.title: Pre-processing
docs.text: Pre-processing turns a list of loops or CTCF peaks into the quantities the Monte Carlo needs: how strongly each bead attracts a loop extruder from the left and from the right.

docs.title: Input: a BEDPE file (loops)
docs.text:
A tab-separated file, one loop per line:

Column Content 1 Chromosome of the first anchor 2, 3 Start and end of the first anchor 4 Chromosome of the second anchor 5, 6 Start and end of the second anchor 7 Loop strength (for example ChIA-PET or HiChIP score); negative values are ignored 8, 9 Optional CTCF orientation of each anchor, between 0 and 1 (0 = forward only, 1 = reverse only, negative = no motif)

Only loops that lie fully inside the chosen region and chromosome are kept. If none remain, RepliSage stops with a clear message.

docs.title: Other inputs: BED and narrowPeak
docs.text:
If you have CTCF ChIP-seq peaks instead of loops, give a .bed or .narrowPeak file. The format is chosen from the file extension.

Format Weight \(w\) of a site Position CTCF orientation (optional) .bed column 5 (score; 1 if missing) middle of the interval column 7 = probability of reverse orientation, or the strand in column 6 (+ = forward, - = reverse) .narrowPeak column 7 (signalValue; the score in column 5 if it is all zero) the summit (column 10), else the middle an extra column with the probability of forward orientation (column 11, or 6)

A peak sits on one bead and adds \(w (1 - o)\) to \(L\) and \(w\, o\) to \(R\) exactly as an anchor does. Peak input has no loops, so the loop figures of the report and PREFERENTIAL_BINDING (which needs loops) are switched off.

docs.title: Orientation from the DNA sequence (motif finder)
docs.text:
If your sites have no orientation, give a reference genome with --motif-genome genome.fa (an uncompressed FASTA; an index .fai is created next to it). RepliSage scans every anchor or peak for the JASPAR CTCF motif (MA0139.1, or your own PFM in MOTIF_PFM) on both strands. A hit is kept when its score is at least the threshold that a random sequence reaches with probability MOTIF_PVALUE (\(10^{-5}\)). For a site with several hits the orientation is

\[o = \frac{\sum_{\text{reverse hits}} 2^{s}}{\sum_{\text{all hits}} 2^{s}},\]

where \(s\) is the score of a hit: the share of the reverse strand, each hit weighted by its likelihood ratio \(2^{s}\). A site without a hit stays without orientation. Orientations already in your file are kept. MOTIF_PAD widens the window scanned around each site.

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
A site is a sharp spike on one bead, but a real CTCF site is not exact to one bead and the LEF legs move by thermal motion. Like LoopSage, RepliSage therefore smooths the profiles \(L\) and \(R\) with a Gaussian of width \(\sigma\) beads (SMOOTH_INPUT = True by default):

\[\sigma = \max\left(1.5,\ N_{\text{beads}} / 300\right)\]

Change it with SMOOTH_SIGMA (--smooth-sigma), or switch smoothing off with --no-smooth. Loops are smoothed with a plain Gaussian. Peaks use a Gaussian whose width is capped (about three times the median gap between sites) so that isolated peaks are not erased. Smoothing keeps the total strength, so the binding energy does not change scale. The number of CTCF sites \(N_{\text{CTCF}}\) and the "legs on a CTCF site" statistic always refer to the raw sites (the second one with a margin of \(\sigma\) beads), not to the smoothed profile. For fine beads, \(\sigma\) in kb can be large; the run log states it, and SMOOTH_SIGMA overrides it.

The replication front is smoothed too (REP_FRONT_SMOOTH, in beads, default 2): the replication time of each bead is averaged with its neighbours and the replicated/unreplicated state is rebuilt from it, so the front is a gently varying profile instead of a random staircase. The start and end of S phase are kept. Use 0 for the sharp front.

docs.title: Hi-C map for validation
docs.text: With --hic file.hic the same region is read from the Hi-C file (needs hic-straw, pip install hic-straw), put on the bead grid and used to validate the model. The bin size closest to the bead size and the normalisation HIC_NORM (KR by default) are tried first; if the file lacks them the next available ones are used, and the log says so.

docs.title: From base pairs to beads
docs.text: The region is cut into N_BEADS equal pieces. For a region of \(G\) base pairs, one bead spans \(G / N_{\text{beads}}\) base pairs. An anchor is assigned to the bead at the middle of its interval.

docs.title: Binding potentials
docs.text:
For every bead \(k = 1, \dots, N_{\text{beads}}\) pre-processing computes two numbers, the left potential \(L(k)\) and the right potential \(R(k)\). They tell how strongly bead \(k\) attracts the left leg \(m_i\) and the right leg \(n_i\) of a loop extruding factor (LEF) \(i\). They enter the binding energy of the Monte Carlo model:

\[\mathcal{H}_{\text{bind}} = \mathcal{C}_{\text{bind}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{lef}}} \left(L(m_i) + R(n_i)\right)\]

Since \(\mathcal{C}_{\text{bind}} < 0\), a LEF with legs on beads with large \(L\) and \(R\) lowers the energy, which pulls loops towards the CTCF loops of your data. Only the shape of \(L\) and \(R\) matters, not the scale of \(w_\lambda\), because \(\mathcal{C}_{\text{bind}}\) divides by \(\sum_k (L(k) + R(k))\).

Building \(L\) and \(R\). Start from \(L(k) = R(k) = 0\) and go through the loops \(\lambda = 1, 2, \dots\) of the BEDPE file. Each loop brings three ingredients:

  • two anchor beads \(a_\lambda\) and \(b_\lambda\), the beads that hold the two ends of the loop;
  • a strength \(w_\lambda \ge 0\), the score in column 7: how strongly the experiment supports this loop (for example the number of ChIA-PET read pairs or a HiChIP score). A strong loop makes its anchors more attractive for LEF legs, and a weak loop only slightly. If your file has no meaningful score, give every loop the same value, for example 1. Loops with a missing or negative score are skipped;
  • optionally, a CTCF orientation \(o_c \in [0, 1]\) for each anchor \(c\) (columns 8 and 9).

For each anchor bead \(c \in \{a_\lambda, b_\lambda\}\) add:

  • Without orientation information, the anchor attracts both legs equally:
\[L(c) \leftarrow L(c) + w_\lambda\] \[R(c) \leftarrow R(c) + w_\lambda\]
  • With the CTCF orientation \(o_c \in [0, 1]\) from columns 8 and 9 (0 = forward only, 1 = reverse only):
\[L(c) \leftarrow L(c) + w_\lambda (1 - o_c)\] \[R(c) \leftarrow R(c) + w_\lambda\, o_c\]

In words: a forward-facing CTCF site (\(o_c = 0\)) attracts the left leg of a LEF, and a reverse-facing site (\(o_c = 1\)) attracts the right leg; values in between split the attraction. An anchor with a negative orientation (no motif) adds nothing. Anchors from different loops that fall on the same bead add up, so beads that anchor many strong loops get the deepest potential wells.

The number of CTCF sites is the number of beads that carry an anchor in \(L\) or \(R\) after aggregation, \(N_{\text{CTCF}} = \#\{k : L(k) > 0 \text{ or } R(k) > 0\}\), so anchors that fall into the same bead count once. If you do not set N_LEF, RepliSage uses \(N_{\text{lef}} = N_{\text{CTCF}} / 2\) extruders, one per two CTCF sites. (Earlier versions used \(2 N_{\text{CTCF}}\); with many CTCF sites per bead that can exceed the number of beads, and then no loops form, so set N_LEF below the number of beads, at most a quarter of it; at or above half of it is an error.)

The input figures show the anchors read from your file: a map (loop arcs coloured by convergent, tandem, divergent or uncertain configuration for BEDPE; anchor strength with orientation markers; orientation confidence \(|2p-1|\), where \(p\) is the probability of a reverse-oriented site), anchor statistics, and the binding profiles \(L\) and \(R\) before and after smoothing.

docs.title: Replication model
docs.text:
When replication timing data are given, RepliSage first simulates S phase on its own: which origins fire, when, and how forks travel along the DNA. The result is a matrix that tells the other models which beads are already copied at every moment.

No timing data means no replication simulation, no forks and only one DNA chain in the model.

docs.title: Input data
docs.text:
Use --rt-file with one of:

Format Meaning Notes .bigWig, .bw Bulk Repli-Seq signal (for example ENCODE) Averaged in bins, log-transformed, smoothed with a Gaussian filter .txt Tab-separated table, value in the third column One value per genomic window .parquet Single-cell replication timing matrix (columns starting with SC_) The shipped file is src/data/replication_timing_data.parquet builtin The shipped single-cell data Covers the chr14 test region; use --rt-file builtin

In every case the signal is rescaled to \(f_i \in [0, 1]\) along the \(N\) beads, where \(f_i\) close to 1 means "replicates early" and close to 0 means "replicates late".

docs.title: From timing to initiation
docs.text:
Averaging single-cell timing over cells gives the replication fraction \(f(x,t)\), a pseudo-bulk timing curve with mean replication time \(\mu(x)\) at position \(x\) (bead \(i\) in the code). The initiation rate \(I(x,t)\) is the probability per unit time that an origin at \(x\) fires at time \(t\). It is assumed Gaussian in time around \(\mu(x)\):

\[I(x,t) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(t - \mu(x))^2}{2\sigma_I^2}\right)\]

with the same \(\sigma_I\) everywhere, proportional to the total replication time \(T_r\). In the code, \(\mu_i = T(1 - f_i)\) with \(T\) = REP_SIM_T, and \(\sigma_I = \lambda T\) with \(\lambda\) = REP_T_STD_FACTOR. Early beads fire first, and a larger \(\sigma_I\) makes timing noisier from cell to cell.

Because a bead can only fire while it is not yet copied, the Gaussian \(g_i(t)\) is turned into a discrete firing probability per step, renormalised as in the paper so that the firing time distribution matches \(I(x,t)\):

\[p_i(t) = \frac{g_i(t)}{1 - p_i(t-1)}\]

This matrix is multiplied by REP_INIT_RATE_SCALE and shown in the report.

docs.title: Forks (Replikator)
docs.text:
At each step every uncopied bead draws a random number and fires if it is below its initiation rate. Not all origins fire: the others are copied passively by forks from neighbours. A fired origin launches two forks (left and right) with a speed \(v\) drawn from a normal distribution,

\[p(v) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(v - \mu_v)^2}{2\sigma_v^2}\right)\]

where \(\mu_v, \sigma_v\) are estimated from the slopes between consecutive extrema of the timing curve \(f\) (REP_SPEED_SCALE sets the scale). Each fork then moves \(r = v \cdot (t - t_0)\) beads from its origin, fired at \(t_0\). Forks stop when they meet, and the run ends when everything is copied. Speed is constant in time, a simplification (see limitations). The check of the model is that the average of many runs reproduces the input timing curve.

docs.title: What the model hands over
docs.text:
Output Shape Used by Replicated-DNA matrix beads by time Monte Carlo barrier and push, 3D sister tie Left and right fork matrices beads by time Figures Initiation rate \(p_i(t)\) beads by time Figures Epigenetic field \(h_i = 2 f_i - 1\) per bead Monte Carlo epigenetic states Initial epigenetic state sign per bead Monte Carlo epigenetic states

The time axis is normalised inside the simulator, before the matrices are rescaled to REP_SIM_T points: the idle steps before the first fired origin are removed, and the simulation stops at the step where the last locus is copied. So the first column of the matrix is the first firing (with its forks, which are aligned to the firing step) and the last column is the moment when everything is replicated. The initiation rate \(I(x,t)\) used in the plots is mapped to the same axis, and Replikator.normalise_time stays as a safeguard that does nothing for a profile that is already normalised. The log reports how many idle steps were removed (with -vv). This only rescales time; the model itself is unchanged, and demo/test_normalisation.py checks it (no Monte Carlo needed). The matrix is then stretched to REP_TIME_DURATION Monte Carlo steps and placed at REP_START_TIME, so S phase happens between steps REP_START_TIME and REP_START_TIME + REP_TIME_DURATION.

docs.title: Robustness checks
docs.text:
The model is unchanged; these are implementation safeguards.

  • Input checks. A missing chromosome, a region outside the timing data, a constant or empty timing signal, or fewer than four data points stop the run with a message that names the problem.
  • Fork speed on smooth curves. The fork speed is estimated from the slopes between successive peaks and dips of the timing curve. If a small region or fine beads leave fewer than two extrema, the region ends are used as segment boundaries, so the speed is never zero.
  • Slow regions. If DNA is still unreplicated after REP_SIM_T time steps, the initiation rate of the last time step is kept and the simulation continues until the region is replicated (the result is rescaled to REP_SIM_T columns as before). A hard cap of 20 * REP_SIM_T steps raises a clear error.
  • Speed. Fork matrices are stacked once instead of at every step. Results for a given random seed are identical to the earlier implementation whenever it finished.

docs.title: Scope and goals
docs.text: RepliSage follows one chromosome through the whole cell cycle (G1, S, G2/M) in a single model, with S phase as its focus. Most tools treat loop extrusion, compartments or replication separately; here the three can influence each other, which lets you test mechanistic ideas with your own data. The paper calls it a proof-of-concept framework, and that is a good way to use it.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Simulate all phases and obtain a 3D ensemble for each, from your own loops (BEDPE) and replication timing.
  • Study S phase: how moving forks affect loops, epigenetic states and sister chromatids.
  • Test hypotheses: fork speed, origin firing, barrier strength, whether forks organise epigenetic states.
  • Model replication stress (RS): slower forks and more origins firing.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text: Phase What the model does G1 One DNA copy. LEFs (cohesin) extrude loops, epigenetic states follow the timing-derived field S Replikator provides fork positions. Forks push LEFs and may organise states. Two chains are tied where DNA is copied and gradually separate G2/M Replication ties are off. A second LEF family (condensin, more processive) and random excluded-volume relaxation (topoisomerase) are added; a gentle force separates the sisters

docs.title: What the paper reports
docs.text:
• Loops get shorter in S phase and shorter still under RS, as in single-cell Hi-C. Cohesin HiChIP under mild RS (aphidicolin, hydroxyurea) shows the same.
  • Compartments stay largely stable under RS. The model's epigenetic states correlate with Hi-C compartments (above 80%).
  • If forks organise epigenetic states, RS gives more B to A switching.
  • The chromosome decompacts in S and compacts in G2/M, as in NucDynamics models from single-cell Hi-C.

Paper settings for chromosome-wide runs: 10,000 beads, 1000 cohesin and 1000 condensin LEFs, \(T_{\text{mc}} = 1.8\), \(2\times10^5\) Monte Carlo steps. The defaults in config.ini are lighter.

For the formalism behind the model, see the Hamiltonian idea. Please read Known limitations before drawing conclusions from a result.

docs.title: The story of RepliSage and the role of AI
How it began
docs.text:
RepliSage was born inside an OPUS grant on replication stress (Polish National Science Centre, 2020/37/B/NZ2/03757), under the supervision of Karolina Buka and Dariusz Plewczyński. The question we started with is easy to say and hard to answer: what happens to the three-dimensional folding of a chromosome when the copying of its DNA is disturbed?

At first there was no model at all, only curiosity. I wanted to start from the first principles of DNA replication, and I wandered through many ideas: the synchronisation of replication origins, chimera states, and other ways to describe many coupled units that fire in a pattern. They were beautiful to think about, but each of them rested on assumptions that nobody could check.

docs.title: The path that worked
docs.text: The most direct road was, in the end, the one next to my own earlier work. I already had LoopSage, a Monte Carlo model of loop extrusion by cohesin. If loops give chromatin its structure, and replication forks travel along the very same DNA, then the natural step was to let the forks walk into the loop model. Extending LoopSage with replication dynamics gave us RepliSage: loop extrusion, a replication programme and epigenetic states, all evolving together under one energy function.

docs.title: It was harder than it looked
docs.text:
I had expected this to be easy. It was not, mostly because the knowledge we needed did not exist yet. How do epigenetic states propagate behind a fork? What really happens when a loop-extruding cohesin meets a replisome? Nobody could simply tell me. Many choices in the model are therefore honest assumptions that we debated, tested, and kept or discarded.

What you see here is the result of years of work and many long conversations with biologists, mathematicians and physicists, who patiently explained their fields to me and questioned mine.

docs.title: Thank you
docs.text: I am deeply grateful to the whole team: to Karolina Buka and Dariusz Plewczyński for their guidance and biological insight, to my co-authors, and to every colleague who shared their time and knowledge. The full list of authors and funding sources is in the paper.

docs.title: The role of AI
docs.text:
Claude helped substantially with the work around the model: reorganising the code, designing cleaner visualisations and reports, and polishing this documentation. I am thankful for that contribution.

The ideas, the equations and the assumptions, however, come from human thinking and human disagreement. If you suspect that RepliSage is "AI slop", I can tell you it is not. One proof is that RepliSage is a perfectly imperfect model: its limitations are stated openly, and each of them marks a place where we did not know the answer and chose to say so rather than hide it.

If you find something wrong or missing, please open an issue. Improving the model remains a human conversation, and you are welcome to join it.

docs.title: A note about the name
docs.text:
There is another project called RepliSage, at replisage.com. It is a 3D scene-replication service for virtual and augmented reality, and it has nothing to do with chromatin, DNA replication or loop extrusion. Please do not confuse the two. This model was first published as a preprint on bioRxiv on 4 April 2025 (doi:10.1101/2025.03.31.646315). We do different things, and the shared name is a coincidence. I wish them a successful journey with it too.

Sebastian Korsak

docs.title: Outputs and visualisation
docs.text: Every run explains itself. This page lists what is written and how to look at it.

docs.title: report.html
docs.text:
A single self-contained page: images and equations are embedded (no internet needed), so you can email it. Only the 3D viewer and movie stay as separate files next to it. Sections:

  1. The model: a short description with the equations.
  2. Run summary: key numbers.
  3. Input: the loop anchors and, with the CTCF occupancy figure, the loop-spanned occupancy profile (0 to 1) together with CTCF orientation, strength and orientation confidence. With --preferential-binding this profile sets where LEFs load.
  4. Monte Carlo diagnostics: energies, energy budget, distributions, autocorrelation, convergence table, running means, stationarity (first vs second half), MCSE vs samples, rolling mean and variance, rank correlations, LEF binding dynamics and compartment domain sizes. Every figure in report.html has a short "How to read it" note. Constant energy offsets are removed (labels start with Δ) so that fluctuations stay visible.
  5. Loop extrusion: the LEF kymograph (one colour per LEF, with the mean loop size over time below), coverage, loop lengths, LEF binding, and the model maps: heatmaps for G1, S and G2/M made from the Monte Carlo state alone (LEF contacts, epigenetic checkerboard and their combination; each caption states how it is calculated).
  6. Replication: forks, replicated fraction, initiation rate, timing.
  7. Epigenetic states and compartments: the state trajectory as a heatmap, order measures explained in plain language (average epigenetic state, synchronisation, cluster order, entropy), the B to A and A to B switching map and the switching trajectory with the replication front.
  8. 3D ensemble: links to the viewer, the inline movies, the structures per phase and the structural-metric figures, including the compaction figure (radius of gyration and hull volume per phase) and the contact maps of the three phases in one row.
  9. Command and parameters: the exact command, the environment, every parameter and the config file.

Every figure comes with a short text: what it shows and what to expect. A sticky navigation bar jumps between sections.

docs.title: viewer_3d.html: interactive 3D viewer
docs.text:
A self-contained page (open it in any browser, no internet needed).

  • 3D structure. Rotate with the mouse, zoom with the wheel. Both sister chromatids are drawn as tubes.
  • Colour modes. Sister chromatids (orange and blue), Compartments (graded epigenetic state, blue negative to red positive), Rainbow (position along the chain), Replication (red copied, grey not yet copied).
  • Markers. Cohesin (green) and condensin (magenta) anchors joined by thin lines (the loops), purple CTCF arrows showing the site orientation, turquoise replication forks. Distant parts fade into the backdrop (depth cueing). Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, right-drag to pan; Auto-rotate and Save PNG are in the controls.
  • Contact map. To the right, a map averaged over a moving window of frames (set the window and the contact radius with the sliders). The top strip shows compartments, the left strip shows replicated DNA, green and magenta dots are cohesin and condensin anchors, teal dashed lines are the forks.
  • Trajectory bar. At the bottom, the whole trajectory is coloured by cell-cycle phase (blue G1, red S, teal G2/M) with the replicated fraction as a white curve. Click or drag to move, press Play to animate with interpolation between structures. The badge on the structure always states the current phase.

Phase indicators. Every figure with a time axis marks the cell cycle: G1 (blue), S (red) and G2/M (teal) are shaded and labelled, with dashed lines at the start and end of S. On replication figures with time vertically, the axis is padded and the bands carry the labels.

docs.title: movie_3d_sister.mp4 and movie_3d_compartment.mp4
docs.text:
Movies take time

The movies are written by default. Rendering takes minutes, so add --skip-movies (config: skip_movies = True) for quick runs. The interactive HTML viewer is written either way and shows the same views.

PyVista movies (mp4) rendered like a molecular graphics program: smooth shaded tubes, ambient occlusion and shadows, and depth cueing (parts far from the camera fade into the backdrop, so they look distant). With MOVIE_COLOR = auto two movies are written, one coloured by sister chromatid (orange and blue) and one by compartment (graded epigenetic state, blue negative to red positive). Each frame has a badge with the current cell-cycle phase and MC step, a legend, and, next to the structure, the windowed contact map and the phase bar with a moving playhead.

  • Cohesin (green) and condensin (magenta) anchors are joined by thin links, the loops.
  • CTCF sites are purple arrows next to the fibre. An arrow pointing along the chain is a forward-facing site (it attracts the left leg of a LEF), an arrow pointing against the chain is a reverse-facing site, exactly as the orientation enters the model.
  • Replication forks are turquoise spheres.

Contact map (heatmap). The map shows a soft, distance-based contact signal of the current window (nearby beads count more, so patterns are not lost in a binary threshold), drawn with a high-contrast colour map and a colour bar. Markers are placed so that you can tell what causes a feature:

  • loop arcs above the diagonal for each LEF (circles = cohesin, squares = condensin), so a loop or TAD can be matched to the LEF that makes it;
  • CTCF ticks on the margins, tilted by orientation (forward or reverse);
  • replication forks: each replicated segment (a replication eye) is a turquoise band on the diagonal between its two forks. Each fork is a diamond on the diagonal and a triangle on both margin strips pointing the way the fork moves (left fork towards smaller positions, right fork towards larger ones), so there are no long lines across the map. A fountain or stripe starting at a diamond points to a fork; one starting at a circle or square points to a LEF.

Phase bar. Below the structure and the map, the bar has one cell per recorded frame, coloured by cell-cycle phase, with the replicated fraction as a white curve, MC-step ticks and a playhead. The playhead is placed in the full trajectory, also when the movie shows only a subset of the frames, and the printed step is the MC step of the current moment (tests/test_video_bar.py checks this).

Frames between two structures are interpolated after aligning the structures to each other, so the motion is smooth. Settings (config file): MOVIE_COLOR (auto, sister, compartment, rainbow, replication), MOVIE_INTERP (frames between structures), MOVIE_CMAP (heatmap colour map: turbo default, inferno, magma, viridis, cividis, rs; the HTML viewer uses the same one). Switch off with --no-movie. The HTML viewer and the movies share one palette (src/viz3d/palette.py), so the colours always agree.

docs.title: CIF files and ChimeraX
docs.text:
ensemble/ensemble_<k>_<label>.cif are standard mmCIF files:

  • one chain per DNA copy (A, and B with replication),
  • one C-alpha-style bead per residue with covalent bonds between neighbours,
  • the B-factor holds the position along the chain.

Open the first file with the script ensemble/view.cxc (in ChimeraX: File, Open). It shows beads as balls connected by sticks and colours chain A orange and chain B gold. For a rainbow along the chain, use

color bfactor palette rainbow target abp

To open the whole trajectory, open ensemble_*.cif loads every structure as a model; use the model slider to move through them.
